category.text: $course$/top/Java Zero-to-Hired/Phase 2/5.1 Resource design, HTTP semantics and status codes

questiontext.text:
A mobile app's 'Send money' call to POST /api/v1/transfers times out after 30 seconds. The app's HTTP library is configured to retry idempotent requests automatically.

Will the library retry this request, and why?

generalfeedback.text: POST is neither safe nor idempotent, so generic clients do not retry it. Payment APIs make it retryable with an Idempotency-Key header that the server uses to return the original result instead of moving money twice.

answer.text: No: timeouts are never retried by HTTP clients
Yes: every HTTP method is retried after a timeout
Yes: POST is idempotent when the body is identical
No: POST is not idempotent, so a safe retry needs an Idempotency-Key that the server honours

questiontext.text:
A transfer request is well-formed and passes validation, but the source account has insufficient funds.

Which status code best describes the result?

generalfeedback.text: The request is syntactically valid but breaks a business rule, which is what 422 expresses. 400 is for malformed or invalid input, 500 for unexpected server failures, and a 200 with an error flag hides the failure from monitoring and clients.

answer.text: 400 Bad Request
200 OK with {"success": false}
500 Internal Server Error
422 Unprocessable Content

questiontext.text:
A customer requests GET /api/v1/accounts/0123456789, an account that exists but belongs to another customer.

What should the API return to avoid leaking information?

generalfeedback.text: Returning 403 confirms the account number exists, which helps attackers enumerate accounts. Responding as if it does not exist (404) gives away nothing.

answer.text: 404 Not Found
200 OK with the balance masked
409 Conflict
403 Forbidden

questiontext.text:
Two support agents load the same customer profile. Agent A saves a new phone number; a minute later agent B saves a new address from the stale copy and A's change disappears.

Which HTTP mechanism prevents this lost update?

generalfeedback.text: Conditional requests make the update depend on the version the client read. If someone saved in between, the precondition fails with 412 and the client must re-read and merge.

answer.text: ETag on GET, If-Match on the update, and 412 Precondition Failed when the version has changed
Cache-Control: no-store on the GET response
Returning 202 Accepted for every update
Using PUT instead of PATCH

questiontext.text:
An outbound NIP transfer is accepted by your service but will only be confirmed by the switch some seconds later.

What is the best response to POST /api/v1/transfers?

generalfeedback.text: 202 tells the client the work is accepted but not finished, and Location gives it somewhere to check. Claiming success before the switch confirms is how customers see money 'sent' that never arrives.

answer.text: 200 OK with an empty body
202 Accepted with a Location header pointing to the transfer, which the client can poll or receive a webhook for
504 Gateway Timeout until the switch replies
201 Created with status SUCCEEDED, then fix it later if the switch rejects it

questiontext.text:
You are reviewing a junior engineer's API design for a wallet service.

Which of these are design problems? (Choose two.)

generalfeedback.text: GET must be safe; prefetchers and retries would move money. Floating-point JSON numbers lose precision; send decimal strings with a currency. Plural collection nouns and ISO 8601 dates are good practice.

answer.text: Dates use ISO 8601 with a time zone offset
GET /api/v1/wallets/{id}/confirm-transfer moves money
Collections are named with plural nouns, such as /api/v1/wallets
Amounts are sent as JSON numbers such as 2500.1

questiontext.text:
A client sends PUT /api/v1/accounts/123/nickname with the body {"nickname": "Savings"} three times because of flaky connectivity.

What is the server state afterwards?

generalfeedback.text: PUT sets the resource to the given state, so repeating it changes nothing further. That is what makes it safe for clients to retry.

answer.text: Undefined: PUT is not idempotent
The nickname is 'Savings', exactly as after one request, because PUT replaces the state and is idempotent
Three nickname history entries and the nickname 'SavingsSavingsSavings'
The second and third requests fail with 409 Conflict

category.text: $course$/top/Java Zero-to-Hired/Phase 2/5.2 OpenAPI-Swagger documentation and API versioning

questiontext.text:
A partner bank will integrate with your new transfers API. Their architects want to review the request and response shapes and error cases before you write any code, and they will generate a client from the agreed document.

Which approach fits best?

generalfeedback.text: When consumers must review and code against the contract before implementation, contract-first works best, and generated interfaces stop your implementation drifting from what was agreed.

answer.text: Contract-first: agree an OpenAPI document, then generate server interfaces and the partner's client from it
Code-first: build the API, then email screenshots of Swagger UI
No documentation: the partner can read the source code
Write a Word document describing the endpoints

questiontext.text:
Your OpenAPI document shows the transfer amount as type: number. A partner's generated TypeScript and Java clients now use floating-point types.

What is the best fix?

generalfeedback.text: Floating point cannot represent most decimal amounts exactly. Treating money as a decimal string in the contract makes generated clients use precise types and parse it deliberately.

answer.text: Remove the amount from the schema
Tell partners to round to two decimal places after every calculation
Change the server to use double so both sides agree
Document money fields as strings with a decimal pattern (for example @Schema(type = "string", example = "2500.00")) and send them as decimal strings

questiontext.text:
You maintain version 1 of a public payments API.

Which changes are breaking and need a new major version? (Choose two.)

generalfeedback.text: Renaming or removing fields and making optional inputs required break existing clients. Adding optional fields or new endpoints is backward compatible.

answer.text: Renaming the response field reference to transactionReference
Adding a new optional response field fee
Making the optional narration request field required
Adding a new endpoint GET /api/v1/banks

questiontext.text:
Your Spring Boot 4 service is configured with configurer.useRequestHeader("API-Version") and supported versions 1.0 and 2.0. A client sends API-Version: 3.0.

What happens?

generalfeedback.text: Spring Framework 7 validates the requested version against the supported versions and rejects unknown ones with 400, so clients learn immediately that they asked for something that does not exist.

answer.text: The request is served by the default version 1.0
The request is rejected with 400 Bad Request because the version is not supported
The request is silently served by the newest handler
The application throws a 500 error

questiontext.text:
A handler is mapped with @GetMapping(path = "/accounts/{id}/limits", version = "1.1+"). The API supports versions 1.0, 1.1 and 2.0.

Which versions does this handler serve?

generalfeedback.text: The plus sign makes 1.1 a baseline: the handler serves that version and later ones until a more specific mapping replaces it.

answer.text: Only 1.1
All three versions

questiontext.text:
Version 1 of your API will be switched off on 30 April 2027. Several merchants still call it.

What is the professional way to manage this?

generalfeedback.text: Machine-readable deprecation headers, advance notice and monitoring who still calls the old version let clients migrate before anything breaks.

answer.text: Send Deprecation and Sunset headers (with a migration link) on version 1 responses, announce the date, and watch access logs to contact remaining callers
Switch version 1 off on the date and let failing merchants call support
Silently redirect version 1 calls to version 2
Keep version 1 forever

questiontext.text:
A colleague asks how to stop accidental breaking changes reaching the mobile app, which is generated from your OpenAPI document.

Which CI step addresses this most directly?

generalfeedback.text: Comparing the generated contract with the last released one detects removed fields, type changes and new required inputs automatically, before merge.

answer.text: Disable Swagger UI in production
Generate the OpenAPI document in the build and fail if a diff tool such as oasdiff reports breaking changes against the released version
Run the mobile app's UI tests manually before each release
Increase unit-test coverage to 100%

category.text: $course$/top/Java Zero-to-Hired/Phase 2/5.3 Standard error responses (Problem Details), pagination, idem

questiontext.text:
A merchant's integration needs to show a specific message when a transfer fails because the account is frozen, and a different one for insufficient funds.

What should their code branch on in your Problem Details response?

generalfeedback.text: Both failures are 422, and detail and title are for humans and may change. The documented type URI is the stable, machine-readable identifier.

answer.text: The HTTP status code alone
The stable type URI (for example .../problems/account-frozen)
The title, translated to the user's language
The human-readable detail text

questiontext.text:
A corporate customer with 4 million transactions pages through their history with GET /transactions?page=80000&size=50 and the request times out.

What change fixes the performance problem?

generalfeedback.text: OFFSET makes the database read and discard every skipped row. Seeking from the last seen key with a matching index costs the same for every page.

answer.text: Cache every page in Redis
Increase the page size to 5,000
Switch to keyset (cursor) pagination over an index on (account_id, created_at, id), returning an opaque next cursor
Add a COUNT(*) query to know the total in advance

questiontext.text:
A client retries POST /transfers with the same Idempotency-Key, but the amount in the body is now 5,000.00 instead of 500.00.

How should the server respond?

generalfeedback.text: A key identifies one logical request. Storing a fingerprint of the original request lets the server detect a mismatched payload, which signals a client bug, and refuse it.

answer.text: Reject it (for example 422 idempotency-key-reused), because the key was used for a different request
Process it as a new transfer
Update the original transfer to 5,000.00
Return the stored response of the first request

questiontext.text:
Two identical requests with the same Idempotency-Key arrive at two instances of your service within a millisecond. Your code does SELECT ... WHERE key = ? and, if no row is found, processes the transfer and then inserts the key.

What is wrong?

generalfeedback.text: Check-then-act across concurrent requests is a race. Inserting the key first and letting the database's unique constraint pick a winner makes duplicates impossible.

answer.text: Idempotency keys should be checked after the transfer, not before
The SELECT should be cached in memory on each instance
Both requests can pass the SELECT before either inserts, so the transfer is processed twice; insert the key first under a primary-key constraint instead
Nothing; the SELECT makes it safe

questiontext.text:
You are reviewing an error response that a customer forwarded to support.

Which items should never appear in a Problem Details response to a client? (Choose two.)

generalfeedback.text: Stack traces and SQL leak internals that help attackers and confuse users. A trace ID and a type URI are exactly what clients and support need.

answer.text: A trace ID that support can look up in logs
A Java stack trace
The SQL statement and constraint name that failed
A stable type URI

questiontext.text:
A partner exceeds its limit of 100 requests per minute.

Which response lets a well-written client recover automatically?

generalfeedback.text: 429 identifies the cause and Retry-After tells the client exactly how long to back off; other codes either look like bugs or like permanent refusals.

answer.text: 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header and a Problem Details body
403 Forbidden
500 Internal Server Error
200 OK with an empty list

questiontext.text:
Your idempotency handler records the key and stored response in one table, and the transfer's ledger postings in another.

Why should both be written in the same database transaction?

generalfeedback.text: Atomicity guarantees that either both the business effect and the idempotency record exist, or neither does, so a retry after a crash behaves correctly.

answer.text: To make the response faster
Because PostgreSQL cannot write two tables in separate transactions
Because Spring requires @Transactional on every controller
So a crash cannot leave money moved without the key recorded (or the key recorded without the money moving)

category.text: $course$/top/Java Zero-to-Hired/Phase 2/5.4 Consuming third-party APIs

questiontext.text:
Your wallet service calls a BVN-verification provider with a RestClient that has no read timeout. One afternoon the provider accepts connections but stops responding. Within minutes, unrelated endpoints of your service also stop responding.

What is the most likely cause?

generalfeedback.text: Without a read timeout each call blocks indefinitely. As traffic continues, every worker thread ends up waiting on the provider and nothing else can be served. Timeouts and a bulkhead contain the damage.

answer.text: The JVM garbage collector is paused
PostgreSQL ran out of disk space
The provider is sending your service malware
Request threads are stuck waiting forever on the provider, exhausting the server's thread pool

questiontext.text:
A call to the gateway's 'charge saved card' endpoint times out on read after 8 seconds. The gateway offers no idempotency key for this endpoint.

What should your service do?

generalfeedback.text: A read timeout means the request may have been processed. Retrying a non-idempotent charge risks charging twice, and assuming either outcome risks a wrong balance. Verify first.

answer.text: Assume the charge failed and tell the customer to try again
Not retry blindly; check the charge status with the gateway's verify endpoint (using your reference) before deciding
Assume the charge succeeded and credit the wallet
Retry immediately up to five times

questiontext.text:
You are configuring retries for calls to an FX-rate API.

Which responses or failures should normally be retried with backoff? (Choose two.)

generalfeedback.text: 503 and connection failures are typically transient. 400 and 401 mean the request or credentials are wrong; retrying sends the same bad request again.

answer.text: 503 Service Unavailable
400 Bad Request
Connection refused
401 Unauthorized

questiontext.text:
A circuit breaker protects calls to the card processor. During a busy hour, many customers' cards are declined for insufficient funds, and the breaker opens, blocking all card payments.

What is the configuration mistake?

generalfeedback.text: A decline is a correct, healthy response. Only technical failures (timeouts, 5xx, connection errors) should count towards opening the breaker.

answer.text: The wait duration in the open state is too short
Circuit breakers should never be used for payments
The sliding window is too large
Business outcomes such as 'card declined' are being counted as failures; they should be ignored by the breaker

questiontext.text:
Your webhook endpoint receives a JSON body and an x-paystack-signature header.

What is the correct order of processing?

generalfeedback.text: Re-serialising changes bytes and breaks the signature; acting before verifying lets attackers fake payments. Verify the exact bytes received, then process idempotently and confirm with the provider.

answer.text: Parse the JSON, re-serialise it, then compute the HMAC over the re-serialised string
Parse the JSON and credit the wallet, then check the signature in a nightly job
Compute HMAC-SHA512 over the raw body bytes, compare with the header in constant time, then parse, de-duplicate by event ID and verify the transaction with the provider
Check that the request came over HTTPS; signatures are optional

questiontext.text:
A payment-success webhook for reference pay_123 arrives twice, and an older 'pending' webhook for the same payment arrives after both.

Which handling is correct?

generalfeedback.text: Webhooks are delivered at least once and not necessarily in order. De-duplicate by event ID and apply only forward state transitions.

answer.text: Process the first success, ignore the duplicate by event ID, and ignore the late 'pending' because state only moves forward
Credit the wallet twice, then reverse one later
Reject all three because they arrived out of order
Set the payment back to PENDING when the late event arrives

questiontext.text:
Your CI build fails every time the payment provider's sandbox is down for maintenance.

What is the best fix?

generalfeedback.text: Tests should be deterministic. WireMock lets you reproduce the provider's behaviours, including failures that a sandbox rarely produces, without depending on its availability.

answer.text: Replace calls to the real sandbox in automated tests with WireMock stubs that script success, failure, slow and duplicate scenarios
Delete the integration tests
Retry the build until it passes
Point tests at the live production API

category.text: $course$/top/Java Zero-to-Hired/Phase 2/5.5 Introduction to GraphQL and gRPC, and when to use each

questiontext.text:
A bank's mobile home screen currently makes seven REST calls on startup and is slow on 3G networks. Each screen needs a different combination of customer, account, card and transaction fields.

Which approach addresses this most directly?

generalfeedback.text: GraphQL solves under- and over-fetching for client-driven screens. Browsers and mobile apps cannot call gRPC directly without extra infrastructure, and bigger REST payloads make over-fetching worse.

answer.text: Adding more REST endpoints that each return everything
A GraphQL backend-for-frontend so the app fetches exactly the fields each screen needs in one request
Replacing REST with gRPC between the app and the backend
Increasing the server's thread pool

questiontext.text:
After adding a GraphQL field recentTransactions on Account resolved with @SchemaMapping, SQL logs show one transaction query per account in every request.

What is the standard fix in Spring for GraphQL?

generalfeedback.text: Per-parent resolvers cause the N+1 problem. Batch loading collects the parents and fetches the children in a single query.

answer.text: Return all transactions in the Account type instead
Disable GraphQL introspection
Resolve the field with @BatchMapping (DataLoader) so transactions for all accounts are loaded in one query
Add more database connections

questiontext.text:
Card authorisation calls an internal fraud-scoring service on every payment and must respond in under 100 ms end to end. Both services are written in Java and owned by your bank.

Which interface style fits this hot internal path best?

generalfeedback.text: gRPC's binary format, HTTP/2 connections, strict contract and propagated deadlines make it well suited to low-latency internal calls.

answer.text: REST with XML payloads
GraphQL with deep nested queries
gRPC with Protocol Buffers and a short deadline on each call
Email notifications

questiontext.text:
You need to remove the field middle_name = 4 from a protobuf message used by several services, and later add a new field preferred_name.

What is the safe way to do this?

generalfeedback.text: Protobuf identifies fields by number. Reusing or renumbering corrupts data exchanged with older clients; reserving removed numbers prevents accidental reuse.

answer.text: Reuse number 4 for preferred_name because the old field is gone
Rename middle_name to preferred_name and keep number 4
Renumber all remaining fields to close the gap
Delete the field and mark 4 as reserved; give preferred_name a new, unused field number

questiontext.text:
A REST facade calls a gRPC account service with a 300 ms deadline. The gRPC call fails with DEADLINE_EXCEEDED.

Which REST response should the facade return?

generalfeedback.text: DEADLINE_EXCEEDED means the upstream did not answer in time, which maps to 504. 404 would wrongly claim the account does not exist.

answer.text: 400 Bad Request
504 Gateway Timeout as a Problem Details response
404 Not Found
200 OK with an empty body

questiontext.text:
You are preparing a GraphQL API for production.

Which controls are important? (Choose two.)

generalfeedback.text: Unbounded queries can overload the backend, and GraphQL errors usually arrive with status 200. CDNs do not cache POSTs, and a public GraphiQL invites schema exploration.

answer.text: Monitor the errors array in responses, not just HTTP status codes
Expose GraphiQL publicly for convenience
Limit query depth and complexity
Rely on CDN caching of POST /graphql responses

questiontext.text:
A fintech must publish an API that hundreds of merchants, using many languages and frameworks, will integrate with.

Which style is usually the best default?

generalfeedback.text: REST over HTTP with OpenAPI has the broadest tooling and the lowest barrier for external developers, and works with standard caches, gateways and security tools.

answer.text: GraphQL, because it is newer
REST with an OpenAPI document
A custom TCP protocol
gRPC, because it is faster

category.text: $course$/top/Java Zero-to-Hired/Phase 2/6.1 Spring Security filter chain and configuration

questiontext.text:
A request with a valid access token for a customer calls an admin-only endpoint.

Which status should the API return?

generalfeedback.text: 401 means 'who are you?' has not been answered. Here identity is proven but the permission is missing, which is 403.

answer.text: 400 Bad Request
404 Not Found in every case
403 Forbidden: the caller is authenticated but not authorised
401 Unauthorized: the caller is not authenticated

questiontext.text:
A configuration contains, in this order: requestMatchers("/api/").permitAll(), then requestMatchers("/api/v1/admin/").hasRole("ADMIN"), then anyRequest().authenticated().

Who can call /api/v1/admin/users?

generalfeedback.text: Spring Security evaluates request rules in order and the first match wins. The broad permitAll rule shadows the admin rule; specific rules must come first.

answer.text: Nobody
Any authenticated user
Only ADMIN users
Anyone, including anonymous callers, because the first matching rule (/api/**) permits all

questiontext.text:
A REST API authenticates every request with an Authorization: Bearer header and creates no sessions or cookies.

Is it acceptable to disable CSRF protection for this API?

generalfeedback.text: CSRF relies on ambient credentials. Bearer tokens sent explicitly by client code are not ambient, so token-based APIs commonly disable it. Cookie-based web apps must keep it.

answer.text: Yes, because HTTPS prevents CSRF
No, because JWTs are cookies
No: CSRF protection must always be enabled
Yes: CSRF exploits credentials the browser attaches automatically, such as cookies, and browsers do not add the Authorization header to cross-site requests by themselves

questiontext.text:
A developer configures CORS with allowedOrigins("*") and says the API is now 'protected by CORS'.

What is wrong with this statement?

generalfeedback.text: CORS relaxes the browser's same-origin policy for chosen origins. Access control must come from authentication and authorisation, and the wildcard origin should not be used for authenticated APIs.

answer.text: CORS only applies to GET requests
CORS replaces authentication
CORS only controls which browser pages may read responses; it does not stop curl, servers or attackers' scripts from calling the API
Nothing: CORS is a server-side access-control mechanism

questiontext.text:
You want a new endpoint that a colleague forgets to configure to be protected automatically.

Which rule achieves this?

generalfeedback.text: A deny-by-default final rule means anything not explicitly opened requires authentication.

answer.text: Annotate each controller with @Secured
Rely on CORS
End the rule list with anyRequest().permitAll()
End the rule list with anyRequest().authenticated() (or denyAll())

questiontext.text:
You are writing tests for a secured transfer endpoint with MockMvc.

Which tests are important to include? (Choose two.)

generalfeedback.text: Negative tests prove that protection works. Tests with security disabled say nothing about access control.

answer.text: A test that the response is 200 for every caller
A token lacking the required scope returns 403
A test that disables security to check the controller logic only
A request with no credentials returns 401

questiontext.text:
Your service needs HTTP Basic for /actuator/ (used by the operations team) and JWT bearer tokens for /api/.

How do you configure this cleanly?

generalfeedback.text: Each SecurityFilterChain applies to the requests matched by its securityMatcher, so different parts of the application can use different authentication mechanisms and rules.

answer.text: Two SecurityFilterChain beans with different securityMatcher settings
One chain that accepts both everywhere
Run Actuator in a separate application
Disable security for Actuator

category.text: $course$/top/Java Zero-to-Hired/Phase 2/6.2 JWT access and refresh tokens, OAuth2 - OpenID Connect login

questiontext.text:
Your wallet API accepts any token signed by the bank's Keycloak realm. A tester takes a valid token issued for the bank's internal HR API and calls your transfer endpoint with it, and it works.

Which validation is missing?

generalfeedback.text: The token is genuine and unexpired, but it was issued for a different API. Checking that aud includes your API prevents tokens meant for one service being replayed against another.

answer.text: Signature validation
TLS on the endpoint
Expiry validation
Audience (aud) validation, so only tokens intended for the wallet API are accepted

questiontext.text:
A developer says JWT payloads are safe for storing the customer's BVN because 'the token is signed'.

Why is this wrong?

generalfeedback.text: A signed JWT (JWS) is only Base64URL-encoded. Sensitive data must not be placed in claims unless you use encrypted JWTs (JWE), and even then it is usually better to keep it server-side.

answer.text: Signatures expire after 15 minutes
A signature proves who created the token and that it was not changed; it does not hide the contents, which anyone holding the token can decode
BVNs are not personal data
JWTs are encrypted by default, so it is fine

questiontext.text:
A mobile banking app needs to call your API on behalf of a signed-in customer.

Which OAuth 2.0 flow should it use?

generalfeedback.text: Authorization code with PKCE is the recommended flow for user-facing public clients. Client credentials has no user; the password and implicit grants are deprecated.

answer.text: Resource owner password credentials
Authorization code with PKCE
Implicit
Client credentials

questiontext.text:
A nightly reconciliation job (no user involved) must call the ledger API.

Which grant fits?

generalfeedback.text: Machine-to-machine calls use client credentials. Borrowing a person's identity breaks audit trails, and network location is not authentication.

answer.text: No authentication, because it runs inside the network
Authorization code with PKCE using an operations staff member's login
Client credentials, with the job authenticating as its own client and receiving only the scopes it needs
Sharing an admin user's password with the job

questiontext.text:
Your service rotates refresh tokens. An attacker steals a refresh token and uses it first; later the real user's app presents the same (already used) token.

What should the service do?

generalfeedback.text: Reuse of a rotated refresh token means two parties hold it. Revoking the family cuts off the attacker, at the cost of asking the user to sign in again.

answer.text: Treat it as theft: revoke the whole token family and require a new login
Issue a new token pair to whoever presents it
Extend the token's expiry
Ignore the second request

questiontext.text:
You are listing the checks a resource server must perform on every JWT.

Which of these are required? (Choose two.)

generalfeedback.text: Signature with an allowed algorithm, issuer and time-based claims (plus audience) are the core checks. Token length and the format of sub are not security properties.

answer.text: The token's sub claim is an email address
The token is longer than 500 characters
The token has not expired (exp) and comes from the expected issuer (iss)
The signature verifies with the issuer's key, using an expected algorithm

questiontext.text:
A back-office web application signs staff in with oauth2Login and keeps their tokens in the server-side HTTP session.

Should CSRF protection be disabled for this application?

generalfeedback.text: oauth2Login results in a cookie-based session, which is exactly what CSRF attacks exploit. Only bearer-token APIs without cookies can safely disable it.

answer.text: Yes: all Spring applications should disable CSRF
Yes: OAuth2 makes CSRF impossible
No: it authenticates with a session cookie that browsers attach automatically, so CSRF protection must stay on
It does not matter for internal staff

category.text: $course$/top/Java Zero-to-Hired/Phase 2/6.3 Role-based access control and method security

questiontext.text:
GET /api/v1/accounts/{number} is protected with hasRole('CUSTOMER'). A tester logs in as customer A and requests customer B's account number. B's balance is returned.

What vulnerability is this, and how should it be fixed?

generalfeedback.text: The role check is correct but says nothing about which account. Every access to an owned object must verify ownership; querying by number and customer ID makes other customers' data unreachable.

answer.text: Broken object-level authorisation: check that the account belongs to the caller (ideally by querying with the customer ID) and return 404 otherwise
Broken authentication: require a stronger password
SQL injection: use prepared statements
CSRF: enable CSRF tokens

questiontext.text:
A service class has a public method transferAll() that loops and calls this.transfer(...), where transfer is annotated with @PreAuthorize.

Is the @PreAuthorize check applied to these inner calls?

generalfeedback.text: Spring's proxy intercepts calls coming from outside the bean. Self-invocation goes straight to the method, so the check must be on the entry point or in another bean.

answer.text: Only when running tests
Only if transfer is private
Yes: annotations always apply
No: method security works through a proxy, and calls on this inside the same class bypass it

questiontext.text:
The update-profile endpoint binds the request body directly onto the Customer JPA entity. A customer sends {"email": "new@example.com", "kycTier": 3}.

What is the risk?

generalfeedback.text: Binding to entities exposes every property, including ones only staff should set. Role-specific request DTOs prevent it.

answer.text: Mass assignment: the customer raises their own KYC tier; use a DTO containing only the fields customers may change
The request will always fail with 400
None: JPA validates every field
Denial of service

questiontext.text:
A teller initiates a ₦20,000,000 transfer. Policy says transfers above ₦5,000,000 need approval by a different supervisor.

Where must the 'maker cannot be the checker' rule be enforced?

generalfeedback.text: Controls enforced only in a UI can be bypassed by calling the API directly. Segregation of duties must be checked where the action is executed, and audited.

answer.text: In the database backup process
In the server-side approve operation, comparing the approver with the maker, and recording both in the audit trail
Only in the web UI by hiding the Approve button for the maker
In the mobile app

questiontext.text:
A multi-tenant banking-as-a-service platform reads the tenant from an X-Tenant-ID header sent by the client.

What is the safer design?

generalfeedback.text: A client-controlled header can simply be changed. The tenant must come from verified identity, and database-level policies add defence in depth.

answer.text: Encrypt the header
Derive the tenant from the authenticated token's claims and filter every query by it (with row-level security as a second defence)
Let each tenant choose a hard-to-guess tenant ID
Keep the header but document it clearly

questiontext.text:
You are designing authorisation for a support agent role.

Which practices follow least privilege? (Choose two.)

generalfeedback.text: Least privilege gives only the access a job needs and keeps actions attributable. Shared logins destroy accountability, and blanket admin rights defeat the model.

answer.text: Support agents get the ADMIN role so they are never blocked
Support agents can read customer profiles with sensitive fields masked, but cannot move money
Privileged actions such as unfreezing an account require a reason and are audited with the agent's own user ID
Support agents share one 'support' login to save licences

questiontext.text:
A team keeps adding @PreAuthorize expressions such as "hasRole('SUPPORT') or (hasRole('CUSTOMER') and @repo.findById(#id).get().owner == authentication.name)" across many services.

What improvement makes this safer and easier to maintain?

generalfeedback.text: Complex SpEL strings are hard to read and impossible to unit test. A bean centralises the rule, can be tested directly, and is reused through simple expressions or a meta-annotation.

answer.text: Remove method security and rely on URL rules
Disable the checks in production for performance
Move the logic into a dedicated authorisation bean (or custom annotation) with its own unit tests, and reference it from the expressions
Copy the expression into every method for consistency

category.text: $course$/top/Java Zero-to-Hired/Phase 2/6.4 OWASP Top 10 and how they show up in Java APIs

questiontext.text:
A statement endpoint accepts ?sort=value_date and builds "... ORDER BY " + sort into a native query. A tester sends sort=(SELECT pg_sleep(10)) and the request takes ten seconds.

What is the correct fix?

generalfeedback.text: Identifiers such as column names cannot be bind parameters, and escaping is not a reliable defence. An allow-list maps user choices to safe, fixed identifiers.

answer.text: Map allowed sort names to known column names with an allow-list and reject anything else
Catch the timeout and retry
Pass sort as a bind parameter in the ORDER BY clause
Escape single quotes in the sort value

questiontext.text:
A merchant portal lets merchants set a 'logo URL' that the server downloads and resizes. A tester sets it to http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ and receives cloud credentials in the error message.

What class of vulnerability is this?

generalfeedback.text: The server was made to request an internal address on the attacker's behalf. Allow-lists, blocking private and link-local ranges after DNS resolution, and IMDSv2 are the defences.

answer.text: Clickjacking
Cross-site scripting
Cross-site request forgery
Server-side request forgery (SSRF)

questiontext.text:
A production Spring Boot service exposes management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=* on its public port.

Which endpoint is most dangerous to leave exposed?

generalfeedback.text: A heap dump is a copy of the JVM's memory, including credentials and personal data. Expose only what you need, on a protected port.

answer.text: /actuator/prometheus
/actuator/info
/actuator/health
/actuator/heapdump, which can contain secrets, tokens and customer data from memory

questiontext.text:
The OTP verification endpoint for transfers accepts unlimited attempts on a 6-digit code that is valid for 10 minutes.

Which OWASP risk does this design flaw represent, and what control fixes it?

generalfeedback.text: One million combinations can be tried quickly without limits. Attempt limits, short expiry and monitoring make brute force impractical.

answer.text: Insecure design / authentication failure: limit attempts per OTP and per user, shorten validity and alert on spikes
Cryptographic failure: encrypt the OTP in transit
Injection: use parameterised queries
Security misconfiguration: hide the endpoint from Swagger UI

questiontext.text:
You are reviewing what a payments service writes to its logs.

Which items must never be logged in full? (Choose two.)

generalfeedback.text: Card data and tokens give attackers direct value if logs leak, and PCI DSS forbids storing CVV. Trace IDs and status codes are safe and useful.

answer.text: The HTTP status code returned
The trace ID of the request
Access and refresh tokens
Card numbers (PAN) and CVV

questiontext.text:
An integration parses ISO 20022 XML payment messages from a partner using DocumentBuilderFactory with default settings.

What should be configured?

generalfeedback.text: Default Java XML parsers can resolve external entities, letting crafted documents read files or make internal requests. Disallowing DOCTYPEs closes XXE.

answer.text: Convert XML to JSON with string replacement first
Increase the parser's memory limit
Nothing: XML from partners is trusted
Disable DOCTYPE declarations and external entities to prevent XXE

questiontext.text:
A message-queue consumer reads payloads with ObjectInputStream.readObject() from a topic that partner systems can publish to.

What is the risk and the better approach?

generalfeedback.text: Java native deserialisation of untrusted data can instantiate gadget chains that run code. Data-only formats with explicit types remove that capability.

answer.text: The only risk is slower performance
There is no risk because the topic is internal
The risk is solved by compressing the payload
Insecure deserialisation can lead to remote code execution; use JSON mapped to explicit DTOs (or at minimum a strict serialisation filter)

category.text: $course$/top/Java Zero-to-Hired/Phase 2/6.5 Password hashing, secrets management, dependency scanning

questiontext.text:
A legacy wallet stores passwords as SHA-256(salt + password). The team argues this is fine because each password has its own salt.

Why is this still weak, and what should replace it?

generalfeedback.text: Salting stops precomputed tables but not fast brute force. Password hashes must be deliberately slow and, ideally, memory-hard.

answer.text: It should use MD5, which is faster to compute
It should be replaced with AES encryption so passwords can be recovered
SHA-256 is designed to be fast, so attackers can try billions of guesses per second; use a slow, memory-hard algorithm such as Argon2id (or BCrypt)
Salts make SHA-256 unbreakable, so nothing needs to change

questiontext.text:
You are moving users from BCrypt to Argon2id without forcing everyone to reset their password.

Which approach works with Spring Security?

generalfeedback.text: Hashes cannot be reversed, so upgrades happen at login when the plain password is briefly available. The prefix in the stored value tells the delegating encoder which algorithm to use.

answer.text: Ask users to email their passwords to support
Use a DelegatingPasswordEncoder that recognises both {bcrypt} and Argon2 hashes, and re-hash with Argon2id when a user logs in successfully
Store both hashes and compare either
Decrypt the BCrypt hashes and re-hash them with Argon2id in a batch job

questiontext.text:
A developer accidentally pushed a live payment-gateway secret key to a private GitHub repository and removed it in the next commit an hour later.

What is the first thing to do?

generalfeedback.text: Once pushed, a secret must be treated as compromised: history, clones, CI logs and integrations may have copied it. Rotation removes its value; history clean-up is secondary.

answer.text: Rewrite Git history and consider the incident closed
Nothing: the repository is private and the key was removed
Make the repository public so everyone can see it was removed
Revoke and rotate the key at the gateway immediately, then check its usage logs

questiontext.text:
A new CVE with CVSS 9.8 is announced for a logging library. Your manager asks within the hour which of your 40 services are affected.

What lets you answer quickly?

generalfeedback.text: Most vulnerable libraries arrive transitively and do not appear in pom.xml. A stored SBOM per build lets you query exact versions across services in minutes.

answer.text: Searching each repository's pom.xml for the library name
Waiting for Dependabot to open pull requests
Asking each team lead
An SBOM (for example CycloneDX) generated for every build, listing all direct and transitive dependencies and versions

questiontext.text:
You are designing how a Spring Boot service on AWS gets its database password in production.

Which practices are appropriate? (Choose two.)

generalfeedback.text: Secrets belong in a managed store with least-privilege access and rotation. Anything in an image or a repository spreads to every copy and is hard to rotate.

answer.text: Use a dedicated database user for this service with only the privileges it needs, and rotate the password regularly
Commit it to application-prod.yml in a private repository
Load it from AWS Secrets Manager at startup, with an IAM role allowing access only to this service's secret
Bake the password into the Docker image as an environment variable

questiontext.text:
OWASP Dependency-Check flags a CVE in a library your service uses. The vulnerable function is in a module you do not call, and no fixed version exists yet.

What is the professional response?

generalfeedback.text: Triage means understanding reachability and recording the decision. An expiry forces a re-check, and the upgrade happens when possible.

answer.text: Remove the library immediately even if the service stops working
Disable the scanner for the whole project
Document the analysis and add a suppression with a reason and an expiry date, then upgrade as soon as a fix is released
Suppress it permanently without comment

questiontext.text:
A KYC service must store customers' BVNs and also find a customer by BVN.

Which design protects the data while keeping lookups possible?

generalfeedback.text: Authenticated encryption with managed keys protects the value; a keyed hash allows equality lookups without decrypting everything. An unsalted plain hash of an 11-digit number is easy to brute-force, and ECB with a key in config is not protection.

answer.text: Store the BVN in plain text with a unique index
Encrypt it with AES-ECB using a key in application.yml
Encrypt the BVN with AES-GCM under a KMS-managed key, and store a separate keyed hash (HMAC) of the BVN for lookups
Store only an unsalted SHA-256 of the BVN and nothing else

category.text: $course$/top/Java Zero-to-Hired/Phase 2/7.1 Unit testing with JUnit and Mockito; test-driven development

questiontext.text:
A test asserts assertEquals(new BigDecimal("1250.00"), account.balance()) and fails with 'expected 1250.00 but was 1250.0', although the amounts are the same.

What is the best fix?

generalfeedback.text: BigDecimal.equals compares value and scale, so 1250.00 and 1250.0 differ. Comparing with compareTo, or a Money type that fixes the scale, expresses the intended equality; doubles lose precision.

answer.text: Compare their toString() values
Use AssertJ's isEqualByComparingTo (compareTo), or normalise money to a fixed scale in the Money type
Convert both values to double before comparing
Remove the assertion

questiontext.text:
An interest test passes every day except on the last day of February in leap years, when CI fails at midnight runs.

What is the root cause and fix?

generalfeedback.text: Tests that depend on the real clock are non-deterministic. Injecting a Clock lets you test any date, deliberately, every time.

answer.text: The code reads the real date (LocalDate.now()); inject a Clock and use fixed clocks in tests, including a leap-year case
Add a retry to the test
The CI server's timezone is wrong; change it
Leap years should be ignored in banking

questiontext.text:
A unit test for TransferService mocks AccountRepository, FeeCalculator, Money, TransferValidator, the Clock and TransferService itself, and verifies 14 interactions.

What is the main problem?

generalfeedback.text: Mock only real boundaries such as repositories, external clients and clocks. Use real value objects and domain collaborators, and assert on resulting state; verify calls only when they are the behaviour.

answer.text: It does not mock enough classes
It is over-mocked: it mocks value objects and the class under test and verifies implementation details, so it is brittle and proves little
It should use @SpringBootTest instead
Mockito cannot mock 6 classes at once

questiontext.text:
A requirement says a debit alert must be sent exactly once for every successful transfer and never for a failed one.

Which assertion style suits this requirement?

generalfeedback.text: Sending the alert is itself the required behaviour, at a boundary you do not own, so verifying the interaction is appropriate here.

answer.text: Interaction-based: verify the notifier mock was called once on success, and verifyNoInteractions on failure
Assert on the log output text
Only assert that no exception was thrown
Do not test notifications

questiontext.text:
You are practising TDD on a new 'stamp duty on transfers of ₦10,000 and above' rule.

What is the correct first step?

generalfeedback.text: TDD proceeds in small red–green–refactor steps. Seeing the test fail first proves that it can detect the missing behaviour.

answer.text: Implement the full rule, then write tests
Refactor the fee calculator before writing any test
Write all 20 tests at once, then implement
Write a failing test for a transfer of exactly ₦10,000.00 incurring the duty, and run it to see it fail

questiontext.text:
Your unit-test suite takes 9 minutes and fails randomly about once a week.

Which changes address both problems? (Choose two.)

generalfeedback.text: Starting Spring for logic tests is slow, and shared state, sleeps and real time cause flakiness. Rerunning or forcing an order hides the problems instead of fixing them.

answer.text: Run tests in a fixed alphabetical order
Rerun failed tests automatically until they pass
Replace @SpringBootTest with plain unit tests for pure domain logic
Remove shared mutable static state between tests and replace Thread.sleep and now() with injected clocks or Awaitility

questiontext.text:
A fee rule has tiers at ₦5,000 and ₦50,000.

Which set of test amounts gives the best boundary coverage?

generalfeedback.text: Bugs cluster at boundaries (< versus <=). Testing exactly on and just past each boundary, plus the smallest valid amount, catches them.

answer.text: ₦5,000 only, because it is the first boundary
A random amount generated on each run

category.text: $course$/top/Java Zero-to-Hired/Phase 2/7.2 Integration tests with Testcontainers (real Postgres, Kafka,

questiontext.text:
All tests pass with H2 in PostgreSQL mode, but the first deployment fails because a Flyway migration uses INSERT ... ON CONFLICT and a JSONB column.

What change to the test strategy prevents this?

generalfeedback.text: In-memory databases only approximate PostgreSQL. Running migrations and queries against a real PostgreSQL container catches dialect, constraint and locking differences before production.

answer.text: Disable Flyway in tests
Add more unit tests with Mockito
Write separate migrations for H2 and PostgreSQL
Run integration tests against the same PostgreSQL version as production using Testcontainers

questiontext.text:
A test configuration declares @Bean @ServiceConnection PostgreSQLContainer postgres().

What does @ServiceConnection do?

generalfeedback.text: Spring Boot creates connection details from the container, replacing manual @DynamicPropertySource wiring.

answer.text: It lets Spring Boot derive the DataSource URL, username and password from the running container automatically
It creates a production database connection pool
It mocks the database so no container is needed
It disables Flyway migrations

questiontext.text:
A concurrency test runs 50 parallel transfers on virtual threads and then checks total balances. The test class is annotated with @Transactional.

Why is this test unreliable?

generalfeedback.text: Test-managed rollback suits simple repository tests. Concurrency and transaction-boundary tests must let real transactions commit, with independent data or clean-up instead.

answer.text: Testcontainers does not support transactions
The test's transaction is rolled back and does not cover work done in other threads' transactions, so commits, locks and visibility do not behave as in production
Virtual threads cannot use JDBC
@Transactional makes tests run sequentially

questiontext.text:
An integration test publishes a TransferCompleted event and then calls Thread.sleep(3000) before asserting that the listener received it. It fails intermittently on CI.

What is the better approach?

generalfeedback.text: Fixed sleeps are either too short (flaky) or too long (slow). Polling until the condition holds, with an upper bound, is both fast and reliable.

answer.text: Run the test only locally
Increase the sleep to 30 seconds
Use Awaitility to poll for the condition with a timeout (for example up to 10 seconds)
Remove the assertion

questiontext.text:
Developers complain that mvn test now takes six minutes because of Testcontainers tests.

Which changes help? (Choose two.)

generalfeedback.text: Separating phases keeps the inner loop fast, and sharing the context and containers avoids repeated start-up. Per-test containers are slow; H2 reintroduces dialect bugs.

answer.text: Start a new container in every test method
Use one shared test configuration so Spring's context cache reuses the same containers across classes
Name integration tests *IT and run them with the Failsafe plugin in mvn verify, keeping mvn test for fast unit tests
Replace every container with H2

questiontext.text:
Several test classes each declare different @MockitoBean fields while also importing the shared Testcontainers configuration. The suite starts many Spring contexts.

Why does this happen?

generalfeedback.text: The context cache key includes bean overrides. Standardising them (or moving mocks into a shared configuration) lets classes share one context and one set of containers.

answer.text: Spring caches only one context per JVM
Testcontainers forces a new context per class
@MockitoBean always disables caching
Each distinct combination of mock beans changes the context configuration, so Spring cannot reuse the cached context

questiontext.text:
Production runs PostgreSQL 17. A colleague uses postgres:latest in the test container.

What is the risk?

generalfeedback.text: Tests should mirror production. A floating tag can change behaviour, defaults or extensions without any change in your code.

answer.text: Tests may silently run on a different major version from production; pin the same version tag
There is no risk; newer is always better
Testcontainers rejects the latest tag
The tests will run faster but less securely

category.text: $course$/top/Java Zero-to-Hired/Phase 2/7.3 API tests with MockMvc and REST Assured

questiontext.text:
You want to check that POST /api/v1/transfers returns 400 with a field error when the account number is invalid, and that the service is never called. The suite must stay fast.

Which test setup fits best?

generalfeedback.text: Validation and error mapping are web-layer behaviour. A web slice test exercises the real converters, validation and advice in milliseconds; calling the method directly skips them.

answer.text: @SpringBootTest with a real PostgreSQL container
A unit test calling the controller method directly with an invalid object
A REST Assured test against the staging environment
@WebMvcTest for the controller with the service mocked via @MockitoBean, asserting status, Problem Details and verifyNoInteractions

questiontext.text:
A JSON assertion compares the entire response body as one string. After a colleague adds an optional field fee, 40 tests fail even though nothing is broken.

What would make these tests less brittle?

generalfeedback.text: Adding an optional response field is backward compatible, so tests should not break on it. Targeted assertions express what each test actually verifies.

answer.text: Sort the JSON keys alphabetically before comparing
Assert only the fields each test cares about (jsonPath / extractingPath) or compare leniently
Delete the tests
Forbid adding new response fields

questiontext.text:
The mobile team's tests mock your API with hand-written JSON. You rename a field; your tests and theirs stay green, and the app breaks in production.

What practice would have caught this?

generalfeedback.text: Contracts make the consumer's expectations executable against the real provider, so a breaking change fails the provider's build before release.

answer.text: Higher code coverage on the provider
Contract testing (for example consumer-driven contracts or provider-published stubs) verified in the provider's build
More unit tests in the mobile app
Manual testing before each release

questiontext.text:
You are listing what a thorough API test suite should cover for a secured endpoint.

Which cases should be included? (Choose two.)

generalfeedback.text: Security and error contracts are part of the API's behaviour. Checking that a stub returns its stubbed value tests nothing.

answer.text: Each documented business error returns its Problem Details type and status
An anonymous request returns 401 and a token without the required scope returns 403
That the mock returns exactly what it was stubbed to return
That the controller class has a public constructor

questiontext.text:
After each deployment to staging, the team wants an automatic check that the main endpoints respond correctly over real HTTP.

What is a good fit?

generalfeedback.text: Post-deployment checks must exercise the deployed system over HTTP. Slice and unit tests run before deployment and use mocks.

answer.text: @WebMvcTest tests with mocked services
Mockito unit tests
Checking the application log for errors
A REST Assured (or RestTestClient) smoke suite run by the pipeline against the staging base URL

questiontext.text:
A test uses @SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT) with @AutoConfigureRestTestClient.

What does this give you?

generalfeedback.text: RANDOM_PORT starts the real server, avoiding port clashes in CI, and the auto-configured RestTestClient sends real HTTP requests to it.

answer.text: A client that calls production
Only the web layer with mocked services
A unit test with no Spring context
The full application running on an embedded server at a random port, with a RestTestClient bound to it

questiontext.text:
An endpoint must return amounts as JSON strings like "2500.00" so clients never parse floating point.

How should a test verify this?

generalfeedback.text: Serialisation is part of the contract. Checking the exact string catches a change to numeric output or a lost scale.

answer.text: Assert jsonPath("$.amount").value("2500.00") so both the type (string) and the scale are checked
Check that the service returned a BigDecimal
Assert that the amount equals 2500 as a number
Do not test serialisation formats

category.text: $course$/top/Java Zero-to-Hired/Phase 2/7.4 Coverage with JaCoCo and static analysis with SonarQube

questiontext.text:
A service reports 95% line coverage. Code review finds that many tests call methods without any assertions.

What does the coverage figure actually tell you?

generalfeedback.text: Coverage measures execution. Assertion-free tests execute code without checking results; mutation testing reveals how many faults the tests would catch.

answer.text: That mutation testing is unnecessary
That 95% of the code is correct
Which code was executed by tests, not whether the tests would detect a bug in it
That only 5% of bugs remain

questiontext.text:
PIT reports: 'changed conditional boundary: amount > 5000 → amount >= 5000 — SURVIVED' in the fee calculator.

What should you do?

generalfeedback.text: A surviving boundary mutant means no test distinguishes > from >=. A test exactly on the boundary closes the gap.

answer.text: Exclude the fee calculator from mutation testing
Increase the JaCoCo threshold
Add a test at exactly ₦5,000.00 that asserts the correct fee, so the mutant is killed
Change the code to >= so the mutant matches

questiontext.text:
A team adds JaCoCo with an 80% threshold on the whole codebase of a 10-year-old service at 35% coverage. Every build now fails and developers want to remove the check.

What is a more workable approach?

generalfeedback.text: Gating new code improves quality as the code is touched without blocking all work; gaming or removing the metric helps no one.

answer.text: Exclude all legacy packages permanently
Write assertion-free tests to raise the number quickly
Apply the threshold to new and changed code (for example via a SonarQube quality gate on new code) and raise the overall bar gradually
Remove coverage checks entirely

questiontext.text:
SonarQube marks a line that builds a CORS configuration as a security hotspot.

What is the correct handling?

generalfeedback.text: Hotspots are security-sensitive code that needs human judgement. Reviewing and documenting the decision is what a quality gate expects.

answer.text: A developer reviews it; if the configuration is safe (specific trusted origins), mark it reviewed with a written justification
Mark it as a false positive without looking
Delete the CORS configuration
Ignore hotspots because they are not bugs

questiontext.text:
You are defining a quality gate for pull requests.

Which conditions are sensible? (Choose two.)

generalfeedback.text: Gates should measure the quality of what is being changed. Code size and commit counts say nothing about correctness or risk.

answer.text: Coverage on new code of at least 80%
At least 100 commits per week
Total lines of code below 10,000
No new bugs or vulnerabilities above minor severity

questiontext.text:
The architecture rule is that domain classes must never depend on web or persistence classes. A new developer imports a controller DTO into a domain service.

Which tool can enforce this rule automatically in the unit-test phase?

generalfeedback.text: ArchUnit expresses architecture constraints as tests that fail the build when dependencies cross forbidden boundaries.

answer.text: PIT
ArchUnit, with a rule that classes in ..domain.. must not depend on classes in ..web..
JaCoCo
Docker

questiontext.text:
SonarQube flags a rule as a 'bug': amount.equals(BigDecimal.ZERO) is used to check for a zero balance.

Why is this flagged, and what is the fix?

generalfeedback.text: A balance of 0.00 would not equal BigDecimal.ZERO with equals, so the check silently fails. compareTo or signum compares numeric value only.

answer.text: BigDecimal cannot be compared; convert to double
Use == instead of equals
BigDecimal.equals also compares scale, so 0.00 is not equal to 0; use compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) == 0 or signum() == 0
It is a false positive; equals is always correct

category.text: $course$/top/Java Zero-to-Hired/Phase 2/7.5 Code review etiquette and pull-request standards

questiontext.text:
You have finished a feature that adds idempotency, reformats every file in the package, and renames several classes. The diff is 2,300 lines.

What is the best way to submit it for review?

generalfeedback.text: Reviewers catch far more in small, single-purpose changes. Separating mechanical changes from behaviour changes lets each be reviewed at the right depth.

answer.text: Submit it with the description 'various improvements'
Merge it directly because the tests pass
Submit one PR and ask reviewers to focus on the important parts
Split it: a formatting-only PR, a rename/refactor PR, then a focused behaviour PR with a full description and test evidence

questiontext.text:
While reviewing, you notice that a new endpoint GET /api/v1/statements/{id} checks the CUSTOMER role but not that the statement belongs to the caller.

How should you comment?

generalfeedback.text: A broken object-level authorisation check is a security defect that must be fixed before merge. A clear explanation and a concrete suggestion make the fix fast.

answer.text: Rewrite the code yourself and push to their branch without discussion
Leave a nit asking for a comment in the code
Mark it blocking, explain the risk (another customer's statement can be read by changing the ID), and suggest an ownership check with a negative test
Approve and mention it in the team chat later

questiontext.text:
A reviewer writes: 'This is badly written.'

Which rewrite is a better review comment?

generalfeedback.text: Good comments address the code, explain why, propose a concrete change and signal their importance. Comments about the person or with no direction do not help.

answer.text: "I would never do it this way."
"Please fix."
"You always write long methods."
"suggestion: this 80-line method mixes validation, fee calculation and persistence; extracting calculateFee() would make the tier rules easier to test. What do you think?"

questiontext.text:
You are preparing a PR that changes how transfer fees are rounded.

What should the PR description include? (Choose two.)

generalfeedback.text: Reviewers need context (why), the approach, test evidence and risks. The diff already shows the code and files.

answer.text: The full source code pasted into the description
How it was tested, including boundary cases, and any rollout or migration risks
Why the change is needed (for example the incident or requirement) and the new rounding policy
A list of every file name changed

questiontext.text:
A reviewer asks you to change a loop to a stream. You think the loop is clearer for this case.

What is a professional response?

generalfeedback.text: Optional suggestions leave the decision to the author, and disagreements are resolved with reasons. Silent merges and escalation over style damage team trust.

answer.text: Ignore the comment and merge
Change it without comment even though you disagree, then complain elsewhere
Escalate to your manager
Reply with your reasoning; if it is marked as a nit or suggestion, it is your call, and if the team disagrees, accept their decision

questiontext.text:
A bank's change-management policy requires that every production change is approved by someone other than its author.

Which repository setting enforces this?

generalfeedback.text: Branch protection with required reviews makes the four-eyes principle a technical control rather than a request.

answer.text: Allowing administrators to bypass reviews
A CONTRIBUTING.md file asking people to get reviews
Branch protection on main requiring at least one approving review (from CODEOWNERS where relevant) and passing status checks
Requiring signed commits only

questiontext.text:
Before requesting review, you open your own PR's diff on GitHub.

Which of these should you remove or fix during self-review?

generalfeedback.text: Self-review catches noise and obvious problems, so reviewers can spend their attention on design, correctness and risk.

answer.text: The tests, to make the diff smaller
Nothing; reviewers will find everything
Debug log lines, commented-out code and unrelated changes, and make sure CI is green
The PR description

category.text: $course$/top/Java Zero-to-Hired/Phase 2/8.1 Git branching, pull requests, rebasing and branch-protection

questiontext.text:
A buggy commit that changed fee rounding was merged to main yesterday and deployed. Several other commits have been merged since.

How should you undo it?

generalfeedback.text: Rewriting history on a shared branch breaks everyone's clones and loses later work. Revert adds a reversing commit that goes through the normal review and deployment flow.

answer.text: git reset --hard to before the commit and force-push main
Edit the old commit with git commit --amend
Delete the main branch and recreate it
git revert <sha> on a branch, review and merge it, so a new commit reverses the change without rewriting shared history

questiontext.text:
You rebased your own feature branch onto the latest main and now need to update the remote branch.

Which push command is appropriate?

generalfeedback.text: Rebasing rewrites your branch's commits, so a forced update is needed. --force-with-lease refuses if someone else pushed to the branch since you last fetched, protecting their work.

answer.text: Delete the remote branch and push to a new name every time
git push --force
git push origin main --force
git push --force-with-lease

questiontext.text:
During a rebase you hit a conflict on the VAT_RATE constant: main changed the value's formatting and your branch added a rounding constant next to it.

What is the correct way to resolve it?

generalfeedback.text: Conflict resolution must preserve both intentions and be verified, because a resolution can compile and still be wrong.

answer.text: Always choose your own version
Abort and copy your files over main manually
Always choose main's version
Understand both changes, combine them correctly, remove the markers, run the tests, then git add and git rebase --continue

questiontext.text:
After an accidental git reset --hard HEAD~3 on your local branch, three unpushed commits seem to be gone.

How can you recover them?

generalfeedback.text: The reflog records where HEAD and branches pointed recently, so commits remain reachable for some time after a reset.

answer.text: Use git reflog to find the commit the branch pointed to before the reset, then reset or branch to it
Run git revert HEAD~3
They are permanently deleted; rewrite the code
Clone the repository again

questiontext.text:
You are configuring protection for main in a payments repository.

Which rules support the bank's change-control requirements? (Choose two.)

generalfeedback.text: Reviews and passing checks are enforceable controls. Bypasses and force pushes undermine traceability.

answer.text: Allow administrators to push directly to main in emergencies
Allow force pushes so history can be cleaned
Require pull requests with at least one approval, including CODEOWNERS for sensitive paths
Require status checks (build, tests, quality gate, scans) to pass before merging

questiontext.text:
A team keeps feature branches open for three to four weeks and spends two days resolving conflicts before every release.

Which practice addresses the root cause?

generalfeedback.text: Conflict size grows with branch age. Integrating small changes frequently keeps conflicts small and main releasable.

answer.text: Assigning one person to do all merges
Trunk-based development: short-lived branches merged at least daily, with feature flags for unfinished work
Turning off CI on feature branches
Longer release cycles

questiontext.text:
You need to write a commit message for a change that adds webhook signature verification to the payments module.

Which message follows Conventional Commits and good practice?

generalfeedback.text: A typed, scoped, imperative subject plus a body with the reason and ticket makes history searchable and enables automated changelogs.

answer.text: updated code
